In spatial data science, we use [spatial graphs](../spatial_graphs/hands_on.qmd) to reflect the degree of spatial interaction between observations. You already know how to represent interaction based on contiguity, distances or spatial regimes. However, in many contexts (notably urban), the interaction follows spatially restricted movement patterns - like those along street networks. In this session, we will cover it, both as a movement through the streets and the one depending on public transport.

```{python}
import datetime

import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandarm
import r5py
import shapely

from libpysal import graph, kernels
```

We start with the data reflecting Census areas in Prague as we did in the last session. The dataset contains relatively granular spatial units with an information about the population living in each, based on 2021 data.

```{python}
#| classes: explore
prague = gpd.read_file(
    "https://martinfleischmann.net/sds/spatial_graphs/data/zsj_prague_2021.gpkg"
)
prague = prague.set_index("NAZ_ZSJ") # <1>
prague.explore()
```
1. Use the name of the census area as an index. This will propagate to the graph itself.


## Walking through the streets

First, we will rely on the `pandarm` package to model interaction reflecting movement (walking, driving, biking) through the streets. 

All parts of the analysis here require you to build a routable network. While you can do that manually from sets of nodes and edges (with edge weights), the most common application is to rely on the street network defined by OpenStreetMap. Given a `GeoDataFrame`, `pandarm` can fetch the data and construct such a network itself, using `pandarm.Network.from_gdf`, as shown below. However, this uses Overpass API, which is currently struggling to keep up the demand (and block bots), so to avoid additional requests, the code below was used to download, construct and save the network to HDF5 file, suitable for multi-component data like this.

```py
network = pandarm.Network.from_gdf(prague, network_type="walk")
network.save_hdf5("data/prague_walk.h5")
```

We can load the saved file directly with the `pandarm`. Download the [prague_walk.h5](https://martinfleischmann.net/sds/spatial_networks/data/prague_walk.h5) file and put it to the folder `data` (or change the path below).

```{python}
network = pandarm.Network.from_hdf5("data/prague_walk.h5")
```

The network is, in principle, composed of two GeoDataFrames, one capturing edges (streets) and another one capturing nodes (intersections).

Edges:

```{python}
network.edges_df.head()
```

Nodes:

```{python}
network.nodes_df.head()
```

Nodes have a special role in the `pandarm.Network`, as the analysis outcome is typically linked to node geometry, as we'll see below.

Second dataset used in this session captures locations of public and private schools across Prague, originating from the [GeoPortalPraha.cz](https://geoportalpraha.cz/data-a-sluzby/5d32db18a5d545a79ad3029917984a89). Read the data and familiarise yourself with it.

```{python}
schools = gpd.read_file(
    'https://martinfleischmann.net/sds/spatial_networks/data/schools.zip'
)
schools.head()
```

To work with the school locatoins within the network, we need to assign them onto the network using the `set_pois` (set Points of Interest) method.

```{python}
network.set_pois(
    category="schools",  # <1>
    maxdist=2000,  # <2>
    maxitems=5,  # <3>
    x_col=schools.geometry.x,  # <4>
    y_col=schools.geometry.y, # <4>
)
```
1. Define a name for this category of PoIs. You will be using it later when referring to this pointset.
2. Define the maximum distance we'll later use in search. Pandarm will use it to avoid expensive computation beyond this threshold.
3. Define maximum number of nearest items we will try to find later. Again, this is to optimise perfomance.
4. Pass the locations as arrays of X and Y coordinates. Note that these need to use the same CRS as the network is using.

### Nearest POIs

Using this, you can find the distance nearest schools. At most, you can find the distance to 5 nearest specified above.

```{python}
nearest_schools = network.nearest_pois(
    distance=2000, # <1>
    category="schools", 
    num_pois=5,  # <2>
)
nearest_schools.head()
```
1. Define the maximum search distance. The algorithm does not look beyond it.
2. Define number of nearest PoIs to find.

The distance is measured from every single node in the network and can be linked back to the `nodes_df`. That allows you to easily visualise the outcome - the map of distance to the nearest school (of any kind) when walking along the street network.

```{python}
# | fig-cap: Distance to the nearest school from every intersection in Prague
ax = network.nodes_df.plot(nearest_schools[1], markersize=.01, legend=True)
ax.set_axis_off()
```

For a better illustration, lets use  a subset of specific schools only. Filter out `'Základní umělecká škola'` which are art schools.

```{python}
art_school = schools.query("TYP_TXT == 'Základní umělecká škola'")
network.set_pois(
    category="art_school", 
    maxdist=5000,  # <1>
    maxitems=1,   # <1>
    x_col=art_school.geometry.x, 
    y_col=art_school.geometry.y,
)
```
1. This pointset is sparser, so we might look further to find the nearest one.
2. We know that we'll be interested only in the most nearest art school.

Get the distances to nearest art school. This time, fetch also the ID of the PoI, not just the distance.

```{python}
nearest_art_school = network.nearest_pois(
    distance=5000, 
    category="art_school", 
    include_poi_ids=True,
)
nearest_art_school.head()
```

The resulting DataFrame now contains two columns, first one capturing the distance, and the second one capturing the ID of the nearest school. The ID is an integer position, not the index this time.

```{python}
# | fig-cap: Distance to the nearest art school from every intersection in Prague
ax = art_school.plot(markersize=1, color='orange', zorder=2)
network.nodes_df.plot(
    nearest_art_school[1], markersize=.01, legend=True, ax=ax,
)
ax.set_axis_off()
```

The ID column can be used to allocate nodes to the nearest school, similarly as is done in the map below.

```{python}
# | fig-cap: Intersections coloured by the nearest art school
ax = art_school.plot(markersize=1, color='black', zorder=2)
network.nodes_df.plot(
    nearest_art_school["poi1"], markersize=.01, categorical=True, cmap="Spectral", ax=ax,
)
ax.set_axis_off()
```

This is, in principle, a Voronoi tessellation based on the distance along street network rather than a typical Euclidean distance.

### Isochrones

Since we have started allocated space to locations based on distance, let's stick to it for a bit and explore isochrones. An isochrone delineates an area reachable via the network within a set time or distance. `pandarm` can help us define isochrones relatively easily (though we need to do some manual coding).

We're going to generate isochrones reflecting approximate 15 minute walking distance (~1200 meters) from each art school. To do so, we first need to understand which node in the network is the nearest one to each of our art schools, as the analysis is tied to existing nodes.

```{python}
art_schoool_nodes = network.get_node_ids(
    art_school.geometry.x, 
    art_school.geometry.y,
)
art_schoool_nodes.head()
```

The resulting series gives as an ID of the node used to represent approximate location of each art school. With this, you can find all other nodes in the specified range, which reflects an isochrone.

```{python}
isochrones = network.nodes_in_range(art_schoool_nodes, radius=1000)
isochrones
```

The output DataFrame is not the most used friendly, but you can see that the `source` column contains repeated IDs of source nodes, with all other nodes within the `radius` and an exact distance to them. Getting the isochrones as polygons, is then a simple GeoPandas operation.

```{python}
isochrones_poly = (
    network.nodes_df.loc[isochrones["destination"]]  # <1>
    .dissolve(isochrones["source"].values)  # <2>
    .concave_hull(ratio=0.2)  # <3>
)
isochrones_poly.head()
```
1. Get a node geometry per each destination.
2. Dissolve nodes to a single MultiPoint based on the source ID.
3. Draw concave hull around each MultiPoint to get the isochrone.

You can now explore the outcome.

```{python}
#| classes: explore
m = isochrones_poly.explore()
art_school.explore(m=m, color='red')
```

If that is of interest, you can furhter analyse and disect the nodes forming the isochrones as they all have the distance. For example, can peel outer nodes to form smaller isochrones without recomputing the routes.

```{python}
# | fig-cap: Distance to individual intersections forming the isochrone
ax = network.nodes_df.loc[isochrones["destination"]].plot(isochrones['length'].values, markersize=.1, legend=True)
ax.set_axis_off()
```

### Network-based aggregations

`pandarm` is also well suited for data aggregations along the network. That can capture accessible population, accessible school capacity or similar questions. Our school dataset contains information about the school capacity in the `KAPACITA` column, so we can try to understand how does the capacity affect the access.

We also have population information linked to census output areas, so we can even ask the question of school capacity normalised by the local population.

First, we need to assing variables from onto the network. Since we cannot add additional nodes to the network, we find the nearest existing node to each point with a value and assign the values to nodes.

```{python}
art_node_ids = network.get_node_ids(art_school.geometry.x, art_school.geometry.y)  # <1>
pop_node_ids = network.get_node_ids(prague.centroid.x, prague.centroid.y) # <2>

network.set(art_node_ids, variable=art_school["KAPACITA"], name="art_school_capacity") # <3>
network.set(pop_node_ids, variable=prague["n_people"], name="population") # <4>
```
1. Get the ID of the nearest node in the network per each art school.
2. Get the ID of the node nearest to the centroid of each census area.
3. Assign art school capacity onto the identified nodes.
4. Assign population counts onto the identified nodes. 

We are interested in the number of spots in an art school within an accessible range per 1000 people. By accessible we mean approximately 30 minutes walking as people are more willing to walk further for specialised needs like this one. However, the furher away we are, the less people are willing to take the trip. We can therefore start with allocating accessible population to each node as a distance-weighted sum.

```{python}
accessible_population = network.aggregate(
    distance=2400,  # <1>
    func="sum",   # <2>
    decay="linear",   # <3>
    name="population",  # <4>
)
accessible_population.head()
```
1. 2400 meters is approximately 30 minutes walking.
2. Specify aggregation function to be `"sum"`. 
3. Define linear decay to make locations furhter away count less.
4. Define the name of the variable we're aggregating here.

This aggregation results in a spatial distribution of accessible population highlighting areas of high population density but a relatively smoothed one. 

```{python}
# | fig-cap: Accessible population within 2.5km along the street network
ax = network.nodes_df.plot(accessible_population, markersize=.01, legend=True)
ax.set_axis_off()
```

We can now do the same aggregation for the capacity of art schools. Again, using the linear decay to account for difference in willingness to walk with the increasing distance.

```{python}
accessible_capacity = network.aggregate(
    distance=2400, 
    func="sum", 
    decay="linear", 
    name="art_school_capacity",
)
```

The acessible capacity then takes into the account locations of art schools, their individual capacity and ability to reach them via street network. 

```{python}
# | fig-cap: Accessible art school capacity within 2.5km along the street network
ax = art_school.plot(color='red', zorder=2, markersize=2)
ax = network.nodes_df.plot(accessible_capacity, markersize=.01, legend=True, ax=ax)
ax.set_axis_off()
```

Now, we can simply normalise the accessible capacity by accessible population to get an approximation of general art school accessibilty. 

```{python}
normalised_capacity = (
    accessible_capacity / accessible_population
).replace(np.inf, np.nan) * 1000  # <1>
```
1. Dividing by zero results in infinity. Replace infinity with missing value. Multiplying by 1000 to get spots per 1000 inhabitants.

The results show hotspots of higher accessibiulity and coldspots of lower one, with some peripheral locations indicating high accessibility, but those schools are quite likely serving a wider suburban region.

```{python}
# | fig-cap: Population within 1km along the street network
ax = art_school.plot(color='red', zorder=2, markersize=2)
network.nodes_df.plot(normalised_capacity, markersize=.01, legend=True, vmax=100, ax=ax)
ax.set_axis_off()
```

Keep in mind that this example is an oversimplification as quite often people will travel across the city using public transport, which significantly changes the perception of distance, as we will explore below.

### Network interaction graphs

The entire idea of accessibility from one place to the other through the street network can be translated into the spatial weights encoding spatial interaction. `libpysal` has a built-in method to derive such weights from a provided `pandarm` network.

```{python}
# this needs new libpysal
travel_cost_graph = graph.Graph.build_travel_cost(
    prague.centroid,  # <1>
    network=network,   # <2>
    threshold=2400,   # <3>
    kernel="bisquare",  # <4>
)
travel_cost_graph
```
1. Points to be snapped to network nodes.
2. The network that shall be used to extract the distances.
3. Maximum distance within which two observations are considered neighbours.
4. Kernel translating the raw network distance to weight.

The resulting `Graph` can be used as any other, for example to derive spatial lag.

```{python}
#| classes: explore
lagged_population = travel_cost_graph.lag(prague["n_people"])
prague.explore(lagged_population)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
# Additional information

`pandarm` is a _fork_ of another package named `pandana`, which was abandoned for years (but is in the maintenance mode now). `pandarm` now contains some additional functionality but all the resources that refer to `pandana` apply to `pandarm`. Simply replace `pandana` in the code with `pandarm`.

For more details, you can check the documentation of [pandarm](https://oturns.github.io/pandarm/) and [pandana](https://udst.github.io/pandana/), the [chapter on Accessibility](https://knaaptime.com/urban_analysis/04_access/simple_access.html) from _Urban Analysis & Spatial Science_ book by Eli Knaap.
:::

## Multi-modal movement

Up until now, we were assuming movement through the street network on foot. However, urban environments are often served by dense networks of public transport, some of which runs on streets but some which does not. To provide more realistic estimation of accessibility and network-based interaction, we shall combine different modes of transport and make full use of public transport. To do so, we need to rely on data capturing public transport schedules in a format named [General Transit Feed Specification (GTFS)](https://gtfs.org). This contains all the information about routes, stops, schedules, transfers, agencies running individual routes and other aspects of public transport systems. For Prague, you [can get](https://pid.cz/o-systemu/opendata/) all this information for two weeks ahead.

`pandarm` cannot model multi-modal movement but we can use another tool - `r5py`. That works similarly to `pandarm` by creating a network object first. Apart from the GTFS data, you need to provide a local extract from OpenStreetMap for `r5py` to use its street network representation to route along. 

```{python}
#| warning: false
transport_network = r5py.TransportNetwork(
    osm_pbf="https://martinfleischmann.net/sds/spatial_networks/data/praha-261020.osm.pbf", # <1>
    gtfs=["https://martinfleischmann.net/sds/spatial_networks/data/PID_GTFS.zip"],
    allow_errors=True,  # <2>
)
```
1. `osm.pbf` file can be downloaded from [Geofabrik](https://download.geofabrik.de/europe/czech-republic.html). This one was.
2. Prague's GTFS data has apparently some issues of missing names of some stops. We can ignore those.

### Isochrones

As with `pandarm`, we can delineate isochrones as areas accessible within a given time from one or more origins. The two packages work a bit differently, so the APIs do not match. Nevertheless, the concepts are similar. In `r5py`, getting the isochrones is easier as there is a dedicated way of doing so via `r5py.Isochrones`.

Let's try to define isochrones around art schools in Prague as we did before, this time using public transport information.

```{python}
art_school['id'] = art_school.NAZEV_ZAR  # <1>

isochrones = r5py.Isochrones(
    transport_network,
    origins=art_school,  # <2>
    departure=datetime.datetime(2026, 10, 22, 10, 30),  # <3>
    isochrones=[5, 10, 15],  # <4>
)
isochrones
```
1. Each dataset linked to the `r5py` network needs to have `id` column with an unique identifier.
2. Provide locations of art schools. `r5py` directly understands `GeoPandas` objects, no need to provide coordinates as with `pandarm`.
3. Specify the time of departure we're modelling as a `datetime` object to 10:30 am on 22nd October 2026. Note that the time needs to be covered by the GTFS data.
4. Intervals in minutes. For each, there will be one isochrone.

The output is a MultiLineString per each time, proviging boundaries of each isochrone.

```{python}
# | fig-cap: Isochrones of travel time (5, 10 and 15 minutes) around art schools
isochrones['travel_time'] = isochrones['travel_time'].astype(int)  # <1>
ax = isochrones.plot(
    'travel_time', legend=True, legend_kwds={"label": "Distance [seconds]"},
)
ax.set_axis_off()
```
1. Travel time is a TimeDelta object GeoPandas cannot natively plot. Convert it to integer representing seconds.

As you can see above, the isochrones are joined together - we get areas accessible from one or more art schools, not a boundary per school. It is often easier to work with isochrones as Polygons, so let's build areas from these LineStrings.

```{python}
#| classes: explore
isochrones["polygons"] = shapely.build_area( # <1>
    isochrones.geometry 
).set_crs(isochrones.crs)  # <2>
isochrones.set_geometry("polygons").explore('travel_time') # <3>
```
1. Use `shapely.build_area` to convert linear geometries to areal ones.
2. Set CRS to the resulting geometries as shapely does not pass it through.
3. Set new polygons as an active geometry and visualise.

### Travel-time matrix

The main use case for `r5py` is computation of travel-time matrices. Travel-time marix contains, as the name suggests, travel times through the network between all pairs of provided orgins and destinations. We can illustrate it by computing travel time from all the census areas in our `prague` dataset to Albertov.

```{python}
prague['id'] = prague.index  # <1>

origins = prague.set_geometry(prague.centroid)  # <2>
destinations = origins.loc[["Albertov"]]  # <3>

travel_times = r5py.TravelTimeMatrix(
    transport_network,
    origins=origins,
    destinations=destinations,
    departure=datetime.datetime(2026, 10, 22, 10, 30),
    snap_to_network=True,  # <4>
)
travel_times
```
1. Again, each dataset linked to the network needs to have an `id` column.
2. Snapping to the network requires points, not polygons.
3. `destinations` are a single-row `GeoDataFrame` in this case.
4. We want to snap the locations to the network.

Here, the result shows the time needed to reach Albertov from across the city via public transport.

```{python}
# | fig-cap: Travel time to Albertov using public transport or walking
ax = prague.plot(
    travel_times.travel_time.values,  # <1>
    legend=True,
)
ax.set_axis_off()
```
1. Using `.values` to pass the underlying `numpy.ndarray` of values. The Series has a different index than `prague` and we want to avoid aligning by index.

However, this can be built as a full $N*N$ matrix, computing travel time between all pairs of census areas. 

```{python}
travel_times = r5py.TravelTimeMatrix(
    transport_network,
    origins=origins,  # <1>
    destinations=origins,   # <1>
    departure=datetime.datetime(2026, 10, 22, 10, 30),
    snap_to_network=True,
    max_time=datetime.timedelta(minutes=30),  # <2>
)
travel_times
```
1. Both `origins` and `destinations` are the same at this point.
2. Setting a maximum travel time to 30 minutes, assuming furhter connections as unfeasible.

Given this is a full $N*N$ matrix, we can directly convert it to `Graph`.

```{python}
transit_graph = graph.Graph.from_adjacency(
    adjacency=travel_times.dropna(),  # <1>
    focal_col="from_id",
    neighbor_col="to_id",
    weight_col="travel_time",
)
transit_graph
```
1. Dropping missing values which are connectoins that take longer than 30 minutes (`max_time`).

With this, we already know how to work.

```{python}
transit_graph["Albertov"]
```

One issue which remains, is that the weight is represented in minutes. We can use the `kernels` module of `libpysal` to convert it to an actual useful weight before generating the `Graph`.

```{python}
travel_times["weights"] = kernels.kernel(
    travel_times["travel_time"], 
    bandwidth=30, 
    kernel="bisquare",
    decay=True,
)
travel_times
```

The code above converts the travel time of 0 to a weight of 1 and a travel time of 30 to a weigth of 0, with a bisquare kernel defining all in between. You can then use the new column as a weight column in the `Graph` construction.

```{python}
transit_graph_weighted = graph.Graph.from_adjacency(
    adjacency=travel_times.dropna(),
    focal_col="from_id",
    neighbor_col="to_id",
    weight_col="weights",
)
```

See that the weights are now as expected for spatial modelling tasks.

```{python}
transit_graph_weighted["Albertov"]
```

This can be nicely illustrated on a map. Notice the discontinuity caused by the locations of public transit stops.

```{python}
# | fig-cap: Spatial interaction weight derived from public transport
ax = prague.assign(weight=transit_graph_weighted["Albertov"]).plot(
    'weight', legend=True, tiles=True, alpha=.7,
)
ax.set_axis_off()
```

See the effects of the spatial graph defined in this way on spatial lag of population.

```{python}
# | classes: explore
lagged_population = transit_graph_weighted.lag(prague["n_people"])

prague.explore(lagged_population)
```

The main routes of public transport are noticeable in the outcome.
